makes one wonder how today's tract developments will look in 1990. If there ever were any landscape amenities, there are few now in the worst of the tracts. The construction was not held; exterior plywood is often warped and unpainted, and in general the houses are deteriorated. Not infrequently there is litter on the ground and in the street, testifying to the lack of care residents feel for their environment.
Where tract subdivision development did not occur, land division has usually been achieved by parcelization. A similar pattern was observed of dirt driveways connecting perpendicularly to the residential streets, and among these driveways are located 7-10 dwellings, built probably on an Ad Hoc basis. These developments somewhat resemble squatters' settlements: built by the residents themselves, often incorporating small gardens and orchards, and very likely better satisfying the residents' concept of community than do the engineers' tracts. Although these rural-within- urban areas do not exhibit any traditional architectural distinction, and appear in violation of housing code standards, they appear to be attractive environments, principally because of their rural elements and their "community-ness".
Amidst the patches of planned and unplanned development occur vacant and agricultural open spaces. These too create a rural atmosphere. A new city park is located on Kammerer Avenue. Interestingly, the park design is highly similar to the park in Gardner. But where in Gardner the park's design blends with the essentially urban neighborhood, in Mayfair the same park seems almost gratuitous, and it certainly doesn't fit the character of Mayfair's semi-rural/semi-urban environment.
Northside CNRA:
The settlement of the Northside area is directly comparable to that of Olinder. Examples of the same architectural styles, lot size, setback, street landscape treatment, etc. as occur in Olinder are present here. And in many isolated blocks, the same virtues and charms exist also.
However, in contrast to Olinder, Northside is a very large project are (approximately 60 blocks); the area's boundaries are not well-drained, so an equivalent place-identity is missing; and several of Northside's streets carry a relatively large volume of traffic.
Thirteenth Street was probably at one time a major auto-oriented commercial strip. The street's importance as a direct connection to the old Oakland Highway has been supplanted by the Bayshore Highway and Highway 17; now Thirteenth street serves a local population.
The other major streets of Northside became important because of city traffic policy. East Julian Street is a one-way westbound road connecting the bayshore freeway to downtown. Similarly Taylor Street also has freeway access; it connects to the civic center area. Important north-south roads include Seventeenth, Tenth, and Eleventh streets; the latter two operate as a one-way pair.
